subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Under the n+1 rule in 1H NMR, a signal that is split into a quartet is caused by:
questions.explain: A quartet arises from coupling to 3 equivalent adjacent protons, since n+1 = 3+1 = 4 lines.

questions.q: An IR spectrum shows a strong broad absorption near 3300 cm-1 and one near 1050 cm-1, with no peak near 1700 cm-1. The compound is most likely a(n):
questions.explain: The broad O-H stretch with a C-O stretch and no C=O peak indicates an alcohol rather than an acid or carbonyl compound.

questions.q: In the 1H NMR of ethanol (CH3CH2OH), the CH3 group typically appears as a:
questions.explain: The CH3 protons couple to the 2 protons of the adjacent CH2 group, so n+1 = 2+1 = 3 lines, a triplet.

questions.q: In mass spectrometry, the molecular ion peak (M+ peak) is used to determine:
options: The relative molecular mass of the compound
questions.explain: The m/z value of the molecular ion peak equals the relative molecular mass of the compound.

questions.q: A compound shows molecular ion peaks at m/z 78 and 80 in a 3:1 ratio. This indicates the presence of:
questions.explain: The 3:1 ratio of M to M+2 reflects the 75.5:24.5 abundance of 35Cl to 37Cl, indicating one chlorine atom.

questions.q: In the 1H NMR of ethanol, the CH2 group is split into a quartet because it is adjacent to:
questions.explain: The CH2 protons couple to the 3 equivalent CH3 protons, giving n+1 = 4 lines, a quartet (ignoring the exchangeable OH).

questions.q: A 1H NMR signal at a chemical shift of about 9-10 ppm is most characteristic of:
options: An alcohol O-H at low concentration
questions.explain: The aldehyde proton (R-CHO) is strongly deshielded and appears around 9-10 ppm.

questions.q: How many peaks would 13C NMR show for propan-1-ol, CH3CH2CH2OH?
questions.explain: Propan-1-ol has three chemically different carbon environments, giving three peaks in the 13C NMR spectrum.

questions.q: Adding D2O to an NMR sample causes a signal from an O-H or N-H proton to:
options: Disappear, because the labile proton is exchanged for deuterium
questions.explain: Labile O-H and N-H protons exchange with deuterium from D2O, so their signal disappears, helping identify them.

questions.q: What does the integration (relative area under each peak) in a 1H NMR spectrum tell you?
options: The ratio of the numbers of protons in each environment
questions.explain: The integration trace gives the relative number of hydrogen atoms responsible for each signal.

questions.q: In chromatography, separation occurs because components have different:
options: Affinities for (distributions between) the stationary and mobile phases
questions.explain: Components separate according to how strongly they are retained by the stationary phase relative to the moving mobile phase.

questions.q: Why is tetramethylsilane (TMS) used as the reference standard in NMR?
options: It gives a single sharp peak defined as 0 ppm and is inert and volatile
It absorbs strongly in the IR
questions.explain: TMS has 12 equivalent protons giving one sharp signal set as 0 ppm; it is inert and easily removed by evaporation.

questions.q: A GC chromatogram can be used to determine the proportion of each component because:
options: The retention time gives the amount
The number of peaks equals the mass
The area under each peak is proportional to the amount of that component
questions.explain: The area under each GC peak is proportional to the quantity of that component in the mixture.

questions.q: In 13C NMR spectroscopy, the number of peaks equals:
options: The total number of carbon atoms
questions.explain: Each chemically distinct (non-equivalent) carbon environment produces one peak in a 13C NMR spectrum.

questions.q: How many proton (1H) environments are present in 1,4-dimethylbenzene (para-xylene)?
questions.explain: Symmetry makes the two CH3 groups equivalent and the four aromatic H equivalent, giving 2 proton environments.

questions.q: In 1H NMR, the chemical shift of a proton depends on:
options: The local electron density (degree of shielding/deshielding) around it
questions.explain: Electron-withdrawing groups deshield protons, moving signals downfield (higher ppm); shielded protons appear upfield.

questions.q: A compound with formula C2H6O shows two 13C peaks and, in 1H NMR, a triplet, a quartet and a broad singlet. The compound is:
questions.explain: Two carbon environments plus a CH3 triplet, CH2 quartet and exchangeable OH singlet are consistent with ethanol; dimethyl ether would give only one signal.

questions.q: A broad IR absorption between 2500 and 3300 cm-1 is characteristic of:
options: The O-H of a carboxylic acid
questions.explain: The hydrogen-bonded O-H stretch in a carboxylic acid gives a very broad absorption spanning roughly 2500-3300 cm-1.

questions.q: In thin-layer chromatography (TLC), the Rf value is calculated as:
options: Mass of spot / mass of solvent
Distance moved by solvent / distance moved by spot
Distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent
questions.explain: Rf = distance travelled by the component divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front.

questions.q: In the mass spectrum of a compound, a fragment at m/z 29 lost from the molecular ion most likely corresponds to:
questions.explain: A peak at m/z 29 commonly corresponds to CHO+ or C2H5+, a characteristic fragment.

questions.q: In the 1H NMR of methyl ethanoate (CH3COOCH3), how many signals are expected?
questions.explain: The two methyl groups are in different environments (one on C=O, one on O) and neither has neighbouring H, giving two singlet signals.

questions.q: The IR fingerprint region (below about 1500 cm-1) is most useful for:
options: Identifying a specific compound by matching against a database
questions.explain: The complex fingerprint region is unique to each molecule and is used to confirm identity by comparison with reference spectra.

questions.q: Which IR absorption is characteristic of a carbonyl (C=O) group?
questions.explain: The C=O stretch produces a strong absorption at approximately 1680-1750 cm-1.

questions.q: To deduce a full structure, chemists combine techniques: mass spectrometry gives Mr, IR gives functional groups, and NMR gives:
questions.explain: NMR reveals the number of carbon and hydrogen environments plus splitting/integration, establishing how atoms are connected.

questions.q: In the mass spectrum of propanone (CH3COCH3), a strong fragment at m/z 43 is due to:
questions.explain: Propanone fragments by losing a methyl group to give the stable acylium ion CH3CO+ at m/z 43.

questions.q: In gas chromatography (GC), the time a component takes to pass through the column to the detector is called the:
questions.explain: Retention time is the characteristic time a component takes to travel through the GC column and reach the detector.

questions.q: How many peaks (signals) are seen in the 13C NMR spectrum of benzene, C6H6?
questions.explain: All six carbon atoms in benzene are equivalent by symmetry, so only one 13C signal is observed.

questions.q: Dimethyl ether (CH3OCH3) and ethanol (C2H6O) can be distinguished by 13C NMR because dimethyl ether shows:
options: One peak (the two carbons are equivalent)
questions.explain: In CH3OCH3 the two methyl carbons are equivalent by symmetry, giving a single 13C peak, unlike ethanol's two peaks.

questions.q: In 1H NMR, the number of separate signals (peaks) corresponds to:
options: The total number of hydrogen atoms
The number of different proton (hydrogen) environments
questions.explain: Each set of chemically equivalent protons gives one signal, so the number of signals equals the number of proton environments.

questions.q: The small M+1 peak in a mass spectrum arises mainly because:
options: About 1.1% of carbon atoms are the 13C isotope
Hydrogen has two isotopes in equal amounts
questions.explain: The natural abundance of 13C (about 1.1%) gives a small peak one mass unit above the molecular ion.
